summary.text: An 11-year-old Black girl was referred to the hospital from a peripheral facility with a one-day history of a non-pruritic rash, abdominal pain and joint pain. Non-blanching hyperpigmented macules involved the hands to the elbows, feet and knees. About four hours after the rash, sharp periumbilical pain with bilious vomiting began, followed by painful, swollen joints impairing walking. A dry cough two weeks before admission had resolved; she had rickets in infancy.

She appeared ill but was hemodynamically stable and afebrile, with joint tenderness and swelling, a soft non-distended abdomen and no signs of peritoneal irritation. Tests showed leukocytosis, neutrophilia, reduced lymphocytes, hemoglobin 11.4 g/dL, normal platelets and an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate; abdominal ultrasound was normal. The presentation was consistent with IgA vasculitis, and several alternative diagnoses were considered and ruled out.

She was started on nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for pain control, ceftriaxone for empirical antimicrobial coverage and omeprazole for gastric protection, with supportive care and serial follow-up assessments. During hospitalization her abdominal pain gradually resolved, the rash began to fade and she regained the ability to walk, while joint pain persisted with improving mobility. She fully recovered and was discharged.
